title: Concurrency in Python: executors and asyncio
seriesTitle: Python: threading, the GIL and asyncio
seriesDescription: Threads, locks, the GIL, concurrent.futures, asyncio, queues and classic drills. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: ThreadPoolExecutor and ProcessPoolExecutor behaviour, Futures, shutdown, pickling limits, asyncio gather, timeouts, TaskGroup, to_thread and blocking the event loop.
source: Python docs: asyncio, concurrent.futures, pickle; FastAPI docs; Real Python; Super Fast Python; Educative multithreading interview course

questions.prompt: Since Python 3.8, `ThreadPoolExecutor()` without `max_workers` uses `min(32, os.cpu_count() + 4)` workers. On a machine with 4 CPUs, how many worker threads can it start?
questions.explanation: `min(32, 4 + 4)` = 8 (verified: `ThreadPoolExecutor()._max_workers` is 8 on a 4-CPU machine). The cap of 32 and the +4 suit I/O-bound work; threads are created lazily as tasks arrive.

questions.prompt: A `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2)` receives 5 tasks that each sleep for 1 second. About how many seconds until all 5 finish?
questions.explanation: Two tasks run at a time: 2 + 2 + 1 tasks need 3 rounds of 1 second (measured about 1.5 s for 0.5 s tasks). The rest wait in the executor queue.

questions.prompt: Match each tool with its main characteristic.

right.text: Reuses worker threads, best for blocking I/O
Runs callables in separate processes, each with its own GIL
Moves one blocking call off the event loop into a worker thread
Runs awaitables concurrently and returns their results in argument order
Structured scope (3.11+) that cancels sibling tasks when one fails
Starts one new interpreter thread per awaited coroutine

questions.explanation: Threads suit blocking I/O, processes suit CPU-bound work, and asyncio suits many concurrent waits on one thread. The last option is a distractor: coroutines never get their own thread.

questions.prompt: Complete the guidance on picking a concurrency tool.
questions.text: Use {1} for blocking I/O such as HTTP calls, {2} for CPU-bound work that needs real parallelism, and {3} for very many concurrent waits on a single thread.
questions.explanation: Processes avoid the GIL at the cost of pickling and start-up time. asyncio scales to tens of thousands of waiting tasks but every library on the hot path must be async-aware.

questions.prompt: Given `executor`, a `ThreadPoolExecutor`, write the call that stops accepting tasks, cancels tasks that have not started yet, and waits for the running ones to finish.
questions.explanation: `cancel_futures` needs Python 3.9+. Without it, queued tasks still run. A `"with ThreadPoolExecutor() as ex:"` block calls `shutdown(wait=True)` on exit, so queued work completes.

questions.prompt: A task passed to `executor.submit(...)` raises `ValueError` and nobody ever calls `result()` on the returned `Future`. What happens?

options.text: The exception is stored in the `Future` and silently lost.
options.why: Correct: the worker catches the exception and records it on the `Future`; nothing is printed or raised.

options.text: The worker thread prints the traceback and then dies.
options.why: The worker survives and keeps serving other tasks; nothing is printed for `submit()`.

options.text: The executor shuts down immediately and rejects later tasks.
options.why: A failing task never shuts an executor down.

options.text: The ValueError is re-raised in the thread that called submit.
options.why: submit returns normally; failures surface only through `result()` or `exception()`.

questions.explanation: Always read the result, check `future.exception()`, or add a done-callback that logs. `executor.map` re-raises when you reach the failed item.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python code print?

```python
with ThreadPoolExecutor(3) as ex:
    print(list(ex.map(work, [3, 1, 2])))
```

where `work(n)` sleeps n tenths of a second and returns n.

options.text: `[3, 1, 2], following the input order`
options.why: Correct: `map` yields results in the order of the inputs, even though the 1 finishes first.

options.text: `[1, 2, 3], following the finish order`
options.why: That would be completion order, which is what `as_completed` gives, not `map`.

options.text: `[3, 2, 1], sorted from largest to smallest`
options.why: Nothing in `map` sorts results in descending order.

options.text: It prints in random order depending on the scheduler.
options.why: Result order from `map` is deterministic.

questions.explanation: `Executor.map` preserves input order (blocking on the earliest unfinished result); use `as_completed(futures)` to process in completion order. Exceptions are raised when the result is reached.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: `ThreadPoolExecutor` can use ever more memory when tasks are submitted faster than they complete.
questions.reason: Its internal work queue has no size limit, so `submit()` never blocks or rejects.

whys.a: Correct: the work queue is unbounded, so the backlog just grows while the workers stay at max_workers.
whys.b: R is the direct cause of A, so calling it unrelated understates the link.
whys.c: R is true, so option c (R false) is wrong.
whys.d: A is true: unbounded backlog is a real production failure, so option d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Bound the backlog yourself with a `Semaphore` acquired before `submit` and released in a done-callback, or feed work through a bounded `queue.Queue`.

questions.prompt: Assume coroutines `fetch_user(uid)` returning a user and `fetch_orders(user)` returning a list already exist. Write `async def order_count(uid)` that awaits the user, then the orders, returns how many orders there are, and returns 0 if anything fails.
questions.explanation: In async code a dependent step is just the next `await`; no flat-map is needed. Catching `Exception` (not `BaseException`) lets task cancellation propagate, which matters for timeouts.

questions.prompt: `fetch_user` is declared with `async def`. What does the statement `result = fetch_user(1)`, written without `await` inside another coroutine, give you?

options.text: A coroutine object; the body has not run yet.
options.why: Correct: calling an async function only creates the coroutine; nothing executes until it is awaited or scheduled (verified: the type is coroutine).

options.text: The user, because the call runs the body to completion on the event loop.
options.why: That needs `await`; without it the body never starts.

options.text: A `Future` that is already scheduled on the loop and runs in the background.
options.why: That would be `asyncio.create_task(fetch_user(1))`; a bare call schedules nothing.

options.text: A thread handle for a new thread started to run the coroutine.
options.why: No thread is created; coroutines run on the loop thread when awaited.

questions.explanation: Python warns `"coroutine was never awaited"` when such an object is discarded. Await it, or wrap it with `asyncio.create_task` / `TaskGroup` when it should run concurrently.

questions.prompt:
A function submitted to a `ThreadPoolExecutor` raises `ValueError("x")`. What does this print?

```python
fut = ex.submit(fn)
try: fut.result()
except Exception as e: print(type(e).__name__)
```

What is printed?

options.text: `ExecutionError, a wrapper that adds the failing task details.`
options.why: `concurrent.futures` has no such wrapper class.

options.text: `RuntimeError, because the work happened in a different thread.`
options.why: Thread boundaries do not change the type of the stored exception.

options.text: Nothing is printed, because errors in worker threads are never delivered.
options.why: They are stored and delivered by `result()`, `exception()` and callbacks.

options.text: `ValueError, because result() re-raises the original exception`.
options.why: Correct: `concurrent.futures` re-raises the very exception object the task raised (verified by running it).

questions.explanation: `fut.exception()` returns the exception without raising it. With a process pool the exception is pickled across, so custom exception classes must be importable and picklable.

questions.prompt: Write a Python coroutine `fetch_all(urls)` that calls the existing coroutine `fetch(url)` for every `url` concurrently and returns the list of results in input order, raising `TimeoutError` if the whole batch takes more than 2 seconds.

checks.label: runs the coroutines concurrently with gather
enforces a 2 second limit via wait_for or timeout

questions.explanation: `gather` returns results in argument order. On Python 3.11+ `async with asyncio.timeout(2): return await asyncio.gather(...)` is an equivalent alternative. On timeout the gathered awaitables are cancelled.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Awaiting three asyncio.sleep(1) coroutines with asyncio.gather finishes in about 1 second.
questions.reason: The asyncio event loop starts one thread per coroutine so that they run in parallel.

whys.a: A is true but R is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.b: R is false, so option b is wrong.
whys.c: Correct: the sleeps overlap because the single-threaded loop switches at each await. There is one thread, so R is false.
whys.d: A is true, so option d is wrong.

questions.explanation: asyncio is cooperative concurrency on one thread. A blocking call such as time.sleep(1) would serialise the three coroutines to about 3 seconds.

questions.prompt: A FastAPI endpoint declared with `async def` calls the blocking `requests.get(...)` and the service stalls under load. Select all valid fixes.

options.text: Declare the endpoint with plain `def` so FastAPI runs it in its thread pool
options.why: Correct: FastAPI runs sync endpoints in a worker thread, off the event loop.

options.text: Use an `async` HTTP client such as `httpx.AsyncClient` with `await`
options.why: Correct: it yields to the loop while waiting for the network.

options.text: Wrap the call in `await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, url)`
options.why: Correct: the blocking call runs in a thread while the loop stays free.

options.text: Add the `async` keyword to the helper that calls `requests.get`
options.why: Wrong: `async def` does not make blocking code non-blocking; it still stalls the loop.

options.text: Run the app with more `asyncio` tasks
options.why: Wrong: more tasks on a blocked loop just wait behind it.

questions.explanation: Rule: never block the event loop. Either stay `async` end to end, or push blocking work to a thread (`to_thread`, `run_in_executor`) or process pool.

questions.prompt: asyncio is a good fit for CPU-bound number crunching, because tasks are cheaper to create than threads.

options.text: True
options.why: Cheap tasks help waiting, not computing.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: a task that computes without awaiting never yields, so it blocks the whole event loop and everything else on it.

questions.explanation: Use `ProcessPoolExecutor` (via `loop.run_in_executor`) for CPU-bound work and keep the loop for I/O waits.

questions.prompt: `await asyncio.to_thread(func, arg)` runs a blocking function in a worker thread so the event loop stays responsive.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: the loop keeps serving other tasks while the thread blocks.

options.text: False
options.why: The function does run in a separate thread, so the loop is not blocked.

questions.explanation: `to_thread` (3.9+) uses the loop default thread pool and copies the current context. It helps blocking I/O; for CPU-bound work a process pool is the better fit.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python code print?

```python
async def ok(): await asyncio.sleep(0.1); return 1
async def bad(): raise ValueError("x")
async def main():
    print(await asyncio.gather(ok(), bad(), return_exceptions=True))
asyncio.run(main())
```

What is the output?

options.text: `[1, ValueError('x')]`
options.why: Correct: with `return_exceptions=True` failures are returned in the result list in argument order, and the other awaitables still finish.

options.text: `ValueError: x is raised and nothing is printed`
options.why: Wrong: that is the default behaviour (`return_exceptions=False`); here the exception is delivered as a value.
Wrong: results are never dropped; the failed slot holds the exception object.

options.text: `[ValueError('x'), 1]`
options.why: Wrong: `gather` keeps results in the order of its arguments, not in completion order.

questions.explanation: With the default False the first exception propagates to the awaiter while the other awaitables keep running; on Python 3.11+ `asyncio.TaskGroup` cancels the siblings instead. Verified by running it.

questions.prompt: Why does `executor.submit(lambda x: x * x, 3)` fail with a `PicklingError` on a `ProcessPoolExecutor`, while a module-level `def sq(x)` works?

options.text: The callable is pickled for another process, and a `lambda` has no importable name
options.why: Correct: pickle stores functions by qualified name, which a `lambda` does not have. Verified by running it.

options.text: Lambdas are forbidden from returning values across a thread boundary of any kind
options.why: Wrong: lambdas return values normally; the limit comes from serialisation to a separate process, not from return values.

options.text: The `GIL` forbids anonymous functions from running inside separate worker threads
options.why: Wrong: `ProcessPoolExecutor` uses processes, and the `GIL` has no rule about function syntax.

options.text: `ProcessPoolExecutor` only accepts built-in functions from the standard library
options.why: Wrong: any picklable top-level function works, as the sq example shows.

questions.explanation: Same rule for arguments and results: they must be picklable. `ThreadPoolExecutor` has no such limit because it shares memory.

questions.prompt: Inside `"async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:"` one child task raises `ValueError` after 0.1 s while a sibling is awaiting `asyncio.sleep(5)`. What happens to the sibling and to the group?

options.text: The sibling keeps running until its sleep ends and the group then raises a `bare ValueError`.
options.why: That resembles `gather` with default settings; a `TaskGroup` cancels siblings.

options.text: The sibling is cancelled and the group silently swallows the `ValueError`.
options.why: Errors are never swallowed; they leave the async with block.

options.text: The sibling is cancelled and the group raises an `ExceptionGroup` containing the `ValueError`.
options.why: Correct: structured concurrency cancels the remaining children, then reports the failures together (verified on Python 3.13).

options.text: The `ValueError` is ignored and the group finishes when the slowest child does.
options.why: A failing child always fails the group.

questions.explanation: Catch group errors with `"except* ValueError"`. Prefer `TaskGroup` over bare `create_task` or `gather` when child tasks must not outlive a failure.

questions.prompt: Ten coroutines each run `"async with sem: await asyncio.sleep(1)"` with `sem = asyncio.Semaphore(5)`, and are started together with `gather`. About how many seconds until all finish?
questions.explanation: Only 5 can hold a permit at once: two waves of 1 second each (measured 2.0 s). A semaphore around the await is the standard way to cap concurrency.
